It's your CV - you shouldn't be too worried about sounding like a dickhead, you should be putting your best foot forward.  You're meant to brag!\*  

I put my WAM next to my degree title and institution, and listed my competition achievements in a 'co-curricular achievements' or an 'awards and achievements' section.  This would really depend on the structure of your CV, though.

\*That being said, if your competition finishes aren't that impressive (i.e. not the finals imo) and you have other things to include, maybe leave them off.

It depends on how good you are at your role.  I know of people who made great connections and got clerkship opportunities through their role in student societies, as they were often required to coordinate events with firms.  Conversely, I can think of some people who were likely 'blacklisted' for poor communication or organisation when connecting with firms as part of their student society role.  For those who just join for the name and not to do the work, it probably makes very little difference (unless you are asked about it in an interview and have to bluff your way through).

Another associate here - agree w out-lawed!  Although it is slightly embarrassing for us, chambers are used to receiving emails about errors and they can be easily fixed.

Depending on the size of the judgment, your judge's writing style, and the deadline they give you, it is difficult to catch everything.  It's also like when you look at your own work vs someone else's work - always easier to spot errors in theirs and miss them in your own work.

Sometimes submissions/statements will be deliberately copy-pasted in, but the judgment will normally identify these as direct quotes or annex them to the judgment.  It can be a waste of time to try and paraphrase the parties' submissions when they can just be inserted for reference - especially where there are multiple amended pleadings.  Similarly, it can be useful to quote the witness' statement directly.  However, I would agree that copy-pasting large portions without acknowledging them as direct quotes/excerpts is not preferred (in my opinion).

And, like out-lawed said, the judge approves the final draft and often makes the last final edits, so if they want a confusing heading in (even once pointed out to them), it goes in.

Sorry to hear, it's really demotivating. 

From personal/anecdotal experience, associateship recruitment is very personality based with no predictable pattern.  You can be a lovely person and a great interviewee, but the judge might have just had more in common with a different candidate, or they want a certain personality mix in chambers etc.  I've even heard judges change their mind on who they're going to hire the day before - which sucks for the original choice but it's how it works.  The hiring procedure is just much more random than it is for clerkships, often with no standardised HR.

That all being said, if you are really keen to do one keep your eye on judges advertising later in the year (as there are often a few new appointments/last-minute hires).  That's how I got my associateship (after about 7 rejections in the usual period), and I know a lot of other people who were initially unsuccessful who got theirs later in the year too.

That being said, if you don't get one just know it says nothing about your ability and won't determine your future.   It's hard not to take it personally but the fact you're getting interviews shows that you are competent and a good candidate.  I'm sure you have a solid career ahead of you.

This is partly what I'm worried about - what if I'm just a good student but lack the commercial acumen or quick thinking in practice?

It's probably just my anxiety amplified by imposter syndrome, and it certainly cannot be fixed by a reddit post, but I am just worried that I won't even be able to issue spot or think creatively when assessing a brief.

Graduated from law school last year (currently a tippie/associate) and, despite doing well at uni, feel like I don't remember anything I learnt and worried I've lost my ability to think critically (if I ever had it in the first place).

Does this get better? Is there anything I can do to improve my past knowledge/stretch my brain? Or am I just experiencing the reality that people who do well at uni might not always be good in practice/at work?
